Identity Erosion.short_definition: The slow loss of your own tastes, opinions, limits and friendships inside a relationship, until the person you were earlier is hard to find.
Identity Erosion.core_meaning: The slow loss of your own tastes, opinions, limits and friendships inside a relationship, until the person you were earlier is hard to find.
Identity Erosion.expanded_definition: Identity erosion is something a person carries rather than something done in a single moment. Over months or years, preferences narrow toward what someone else likes, old friendships fade, and your own needs and limits are set aside to keep the peace. Self-abandonment names this very pattern from the inside, so this entry covers both. Everyone changes in a close relationship, and some of it is welcome. The concern is change that runs one way, that you did not choose, and that leaves you unsure what you would pick alone.
Identity Erosion.plain_language_summary: You look up and cannot say what you like, what you think or where your limits are, because most of it has been bent around keeping someone else content.
Identity Erosion.why_this_matters: You can say what would keep the peace far more readily than what you want, and your own limits stop being information you are willing to act on. That makes it harder to judge a situation, to describe what you need, or to reach the people who could help.
what_it_is: A gradual shift in tastes, opinions, clothes, hobbies and routines toward another person's.
Agreeing to things you promised yourself beforehand you would not agree to, then treating your own tiredness or need for rest as something to hide.
A shrinking circle, in which friends and family are seen less because there is less room or less welcome for them.
Often a run of small accommodations, each reasonable alone, that add up to a different life.
A state felt from the inside, usually noticed later when a song or a photo shows the gap.
what_it_sounds_like: "I don't know, whatever you want is fine."
"I used to love painting, but I haven't picked up a brush in years."
"I haven't seen my college friends since we moved in together. It just sort of happened."
"What do I think about it? I'd have to check what we think."
"I can tell you what would keep things calm. I can't tell you what I want."
Finding an old playlist and not recognizing a single song as yours.
"I swore I would not say yes to that again, and I just said yes."
"I can't remember what I wore before I met them."
what_it_is_not: Growing and changing in a good partnership, where both people try new things and both keep parts of their old selves.
A move, a new job or a new baby that naturally replaces old routines and friends for a while.
Falling out of an old hobby because you lost interest, with nobody encouraging that.
Ordinary compromise, which is mutual and bounded: each person gives something up and both can say what.
Putting a partner's urgent need first during an illness or crisis, then returning to your own baseline afterwards.
The ordinary blur of early adulthood, when many people are still working out who they are.
this_may_be_it_when: You can name specific things you loved before the relationship that you now avoid or feel awkward about.
You pre-check how a friend, hobby or opinion will be received before you act on it.
You agree out loud with views you privately do not hold, mostly to avoid a bad reaction.
Your own exhaustion, limits or wishes feel like problems to hide rather than information to use.
Imagining a day entirely on your own leaves you unsure what you would do with it.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can say why each change happened and would make the same choice again.
Your old friends are still in your life, though you see them less because of distance.
You have taken on your partner's hobby and still do things that only you enjoy.
Your views have shifted because you thought them through, and you can argue for them.
Changes are matched by your partner's own changes, and both of you say the relationship has made you more yourself.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Taste and opinion shift naturally across a decade, relationship or not.
Partners often trade interests and enjoy it.
A busy stage of life, with young children or demanding work, pushes out hobbies and friendships for reasons that involve nobody's influence.
Someone coming out of a difficult stretch may be rebuilding their sense of self slowly.
common_false_positives: Moving across the country and losing daily contact with old friends.
Giving up an old sport after an injury.
Choosing a quieter life after years of being very social, and being glad of it.
discernment_questions: Can you list three things you liked before this relationship that you no longer do, and do you miss them?
Who decided that those things should change, and did you agree at the time?
If you were making plans only for yourself, what would you pick?
Is anyone else bending toward your needs as much as you bend toward theirs?
When you express an opinion, do you check first how it will land?
less_concerning_if: You can still say what you like and think, even when it differs from your partner's.
Your friendships continue, in some form, and are welcome in the home.
You enjoy the new habits and can trace how you came to them.
more_concerning_if: Your own preferences are met with sighs, mockery or silence, so you stop voicing them.
Money, transport or schedules are arranged so that you cannot easily see other people.
You are afraid to say what you actually want, even in small matters.
pattern_over_time_signs: Photos from a few years ago look like someone you would have to introduce to new friends.
Your answer to "what do you want to do?" starts with a pause and the other person's name.
You find yourself defending the changes when a friend asks about them, before they have criticized anything.
Small pleasures that were yours alone, such as a morning run or a book club, drop away without a decision.
Identity Erosion.repair_check: Look for small pieces of you coming back: a hobby picked up again, a friend called, an opinion said aloud that survived. Rebuilding tends to arrive in acts like these. A weekend of reinvention that fades by Monday is not the same, and neither is a promise from someone else to give you more space.
Identity Erosion.boundary_respect_check: Try one small choice that is only yours, such as a meal, a song or a Saturday plan, and watch what follows. Does it simply stand? Or does a habit of checking first take over before you notice, and does anyone answer your choice with a sigh or a silence?
Identity Erosion.psychological_mechanism: Adapting to another person's likes and moods can be a way of keeping a relationship steady, and it tends to feel like love or flexibility while it is happening. Each accommodation is small, so no single one prompts a second look. Over time a person's own preferences get less practice and can become harder to hear.
Identity Erosion.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe an odd grief for someone who is still alive, a flatness when asked what they like, and a fear that nothing of them is left. Some say the loss showed itself only after the relationship ended, when the quiet gave them no cues. Guilt for even noticing it is common.

response_options.soft_clarification: Share one small, specific thing aloud and see how it is received before deciding what to share next: "I miss my pottery class. I'd like to go back on Thursdays."
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep one thing as yours without making an announcement of it, such as a weekly call with a friend, and treat it as settled for yourself.
response_options.disengagement: Take small steps back toward things that were yours, such as a long-ignored hobby, at a pace that feels safe, and let them rebuild without needing anyone's permission.
response_options.support_seeking: Get in touch with one old friend or relative and ask what they remember about you. Their account can help you recover your own.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If this is happening at work, such as on a team that rewards sameness, keep notes on the projects and ideas that were yours, and talk to a mentor about reclaiming them.

Identity Erosion.boundary_script: Self-support script: "What I like and think counts, even when I can't say it out loud yet. I can start with one small choice today that is only mine."
Identity Erosion.safety_note: Watch for signs that the narrowing is enforced rather than drifted into: friends, money, phone or travel being limited, or days of anger or silence when you disagree. If any of that is present, a domestic abuse advocate can help you plan privately, at a pace and on a device that are safe for you, before anything is raised with the other person.
misuse_warning: Telling a friend that they have lost themselves in a relationship, when they say they are happy, can feel like a verdict and push them away. Offer your observation once and keep the door open.
Using the phrase to explain every change in a partner, such as a new hobby, can turn growth into a charge against the person they love.
Identity Erosion.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Fawning is appeasing a person who feels threatening, as a way of staying safe, and it can happen in a single tense moment. Identity erosion is the long-term residue: the likes, limits and friends that went missing. Self-Gaslighting Induction is the habit of doubting your own memory and perception, whereas here what has faded is knowing what you want. Identity Hooking has someone claim your achievements as theirs, which this does not require.

Public Humiliation.short_definition: Embarrassing or belittling a person in front of others, or putting their private matters on show, so the audience adds to the sting.
Public Humiliation.core_meaning: Embarrassing or belittling a person in front of others, or putting their private matters on show, so the audience adds to the sting.
Public Humiliation.expanded_definition: Public humiliation is a correction, joke, revealed secret, story or post aimed at one person where others can see or hear it. Public exposure is this tactic under another name, so this entry covers both. Feedback given in company is sometimes unavoidable, so context matters. It raises concern when the audience seems to be part of the point, when the same words would be gentler in private, and when it keeps landing on one person.
Public Humiliation.plain_language_summary: You are put down, corrected, laughed at or have something private shown to others, in a way that would have been handled differently one on one. The audience is what makes it hurt.
Public Humiliation.why_this_matters: An audience makes the injury durable in a way private criticism is not: everyone present carries a version of it afterwards, including the person it was about. It cannot be taken back privately later, and it can change how the group treats you.
what_it_is: Criticism, ridicule or private information put on show where other people can see or hear it.
Forms include a correction in a meeting, a story told against you at dinner, a group message quoting your private words, or a post that names you.
More lasting than a private remark, because witnesses remember it and the target remembers them remembering.
Seen in workplaces, classrooms, families, friend groups and online.
Sometimes the venue is the one with the largest audience, such as an all-staff call or a holiday table, when a quiet word was available.
what_it_sounds_like: "Let me show everyone how it should have been done."
"Tell them what you did last weekend. Go on, it's hilarious."
A manager reading out your error on a team call, with your name attached.
"Oh, don't mind her, she never gets the details right."
A group chat message that quotes something private you said, followed by laughing faces.
"Do you want to tell them, or shall I?"
"Since we're all here, we might as well go through your review."
what_it_is_not: Necessary, time-sensitive feedback that has to be given where others happen to be, such as a safety problem in a room full of people.
Settings where feedback is normal and applied evenly to everybody, such as a design critique, which humiliate nobody.
An awkward moment that was only poor timing, or carelessness with something private, such as an offhand mention at a party.
A public award or roast that the person agreed to and enjoys.
Information that is public for a real, disclosed reason, such as a published result or a minuted decision.
A story told with affection that the person is happy to have told, and might tell themselves.
this_may_be_it_when: The criticism is harsher with people around than when you are alone together.
Private things, such as a mistake, a diagnosis or a secret, are brought out in front of others.
The same person is picked out in group settings more than anyone else is.
A quiet word would have been easy to arrange and was never tried.
Others glance at you or look away afterwards, and the room seems to settle on you as the joke.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The feedback is the same for everyone and given in a way that is meant to be useful.
It was an emergency or a safety issue that needed fixing straight away.
You agreed to the format, such as a review session where all work is critiqued.
The speaker followed up privately to check how you felt and repaired it.
The comment was clumsy but kind in tone, and the person was visibly sorry.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A busy meeting or live session leaves no time for private notes, and a quick correction may be the only option.
Some cultures and teams treat open correction as normal and respectful.
A person telling a funny story may not realize you find it embarrassing.
common_false_positives: A choir director correcting a section's timing.
A friend sharing an old photo that you also find funny now.
A manager reading out a company-wide error without naming anyone.
discernment_questions: Would the same words have been said in private, in the same way?
Did the audience seem to matter to the person speaking?
Is the same person the target again and again?
Was anything I had told in confidence used?
After it happened, did the person check in or acknowledge it?
less_concerning_if: Everyone is treated the same, and the setting makes public correction expected.
The person speaks to you in private afterward and makes it right.
The topic was a work task, and no personal detail was used.
more_concerning_if: Private information, like health, money or family trouble, is brought out in front of others.
The audience is the one that matters most to you, such as your family, your team or your online followers.
Mentioning it leads to more of it, or to being told you embarrassed yourself.
pattern_over_time_signs: You begin to dread gatherings, meetings or group chats where this person will be present.
You prepare your answers in advance, to avoid being caught out in front of others.
Other people start to treat you as the butt of the joke, taking their cue from the way you are treated.
You speak less in groups, and your contributions are noticed less.
Public Humiliation.repair_check: Meaningful change would show in public as well as in private: the person corrects you, if they must, in a way that does not expose you, and speaks up for you when others laugh. Apologizing in a private message while repeating the behavior in front of others leaves the audience part unchanged.
Public Humiliation.boundary_respect_check: Ask for correction to happen one on one, then see what the next group setting brings. Is your request kept when other people are present, which is the moment it matters most? Or does the next public remark show it was put aside?
Public Humiliation.psychological_mechanism: People are highly attuned to how their group sees them, and being lowered in front of others is a hit to standing, not only to feelings. Witnesses add to it by laughing, going quiet or looking away. A person may begin to expect it, and the dread alone can change how they speak and act around others.
Public Humiliation.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe heat in the face, loss of words, replaying the moment for days, and avoiding the people who saw it. Some say the worst part was a bystander's silence. Many talk about shrinking in later meetings, and about checking whether anyone still remembers.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for privacy next time, in a matter-of-fact tone: "If there's a problem with my work, I'd find it easier to hear it one on one."
response_options.firm_boundary: Name it lightly, in the moment if you can: "That was hard to hear in front of everyone. Could we pick it up later, just the two of us?"
response_options.disengagement: Leave the room, the chat or the table for a few minutes without explanation, and return only when the subject has moved on.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk to someone who was there, and ask what they saw and heard. Knowing that a witness found it unfair can lift the doubt you carry.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Write down the date, the setting, the words used and who was present, then take the record to HR, a union rep, or a manager one level up.

Public Humiliation.boundary_script: "I'm glad to hear your feedback on my work. I'd just like to have it in private, not in front of the team."
Public Humiliation.safety_note: Humiliation is mostly about standing and dignity, but it can sit alongside danger when it involves intimate images or private details shared without consent, hints that something will be revealed unless you comply, or exposure that follows you from the household into work or online spaces. Save dated screenshots, and ask a legal aid service or an advocate who handles image-based or domestic abuse about next steps before replying.
misuse_warning: Calling a fair, public correction humiliation can let real problems with performance go unaddressed. The label fits when the audience is the point, not when the venue is.
Telling a group that someone humiliated you, as a way to turn people against them, can become a humiliation of its own.
Public Humiliation.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Shame Installation works on your sense of being fundamentally inadequate and can happen in private, whereas this relies on witnesses. A Smear Campaign spreads distorted claims about you to build a reputation over time; public humiliation is a moment played to the people in the room or the group chat. Humiliation Rituals dress the degradation as initiation or discipline and say the pain proves it is working.

Setting Up to Fail.short_definition: Giving someone a task or a standard they are unlikely to meet under the conditions provided, then treating the shortfall as proof of their inadequacy.
Setting Up to Fail.core_meaning: Giving someone a task or a standard they are unlikely to meet under the conditions provided, then treating the shortfall as proof of their inadequacy.
Setting Up to Fail.expanded_definition: This covers two shapes: one assignment with the odds stacked, such as a deadline too short, a budget too small or information held back, and a standing bar kept out of reach by vague, shifting or contradictory criteria. Impossible metrics is just this tactic seen in its standing-bar form, so this entry covers both. Hard tasks are normal. The pattern shows when requests for what is needed are brushed aside, the finish line moves, and the miss is later cited as a fact about you.
Setting Up to Fail.plain_language_summary: You get a job or a target that few people could meet with what you were given, and when you fall short, the blame lands on you and not on the set-up.
Setting Up to Fail.why_this_matters: Conditions disappear from the account and only the outcome remains, so a predictable failure becomes durable evidence about the person who was handed it. Effort rises while the record of misses grows, and that record can be quoted in reviews and decisions about you long after the conditions are forgotten.
what_it_is: A single task whose conditions make success unlikely: an impossible timeline, a thin budget, no access to people or data.
A standing target whose criteria, such as 'be more strategic', are vague enough to be reread after the fact.
A number that rises just as you approach it, or a new condition added when you meet the old one.
Contradictory demands, like cutting costs and doubling quality with the same team and hours.
A retelling that drops the conditions: 'the launch failed' instead of 'the launch had two weeks and no designer'.
Found in jobs, schools, households and caregiving, wherever one person sets the terms and another is judged on them.
what_it_sounds_like: "I know it's due Friday and the data isn't in yet, but I have faith in you."
"There's no budget for that, just make it work."
"You don't need to see the client brief. Just draft it."
"Hit ninety-five percent and we'll talk." Then, once you do: "Now we need ninety-eight."
"It just needs to be more polished," with no description of what polished means.
"I want it fast, perfect and cheap, and I'm not discussing which one gives."
"Why did you let it fail? I gave you everything you needed."
"Remember the Henderson project? That's why I can't trust you with this."
what_it_is_not: Hard tasks with real constraints, which are ordinary work, and resources that are unavailable to everyone rather than withheld from you.
Something that turned out harder than anyone anticipated, with nobody having arranged it.
A stretch goal or pilot framed openly as aspirational, with a fallback in place, so a miss is understood to be fine.
A demanding bar that others in your role have met under the same conditions, or that you have cleared before.
Clumsy delegation by someone who underestimated the task and revises the plan when told.
Hard but specific performance management, with written criteria and support.
this_may_be_it_when: Asked for what you need, you get a refusal without a reason.
Others got more time or support on comparable tasks.
Nobody under similar conditions has met the bar, and the goal changes shape just as you near it.
Asked what success looks like, you get adjectives instead of numbers or examples.
The record afterwards leaves out the constraints you flagged, and lists your misses more carefully than your hits.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You and the person assigning it both knew the odds and agreed to go ahead for a stated reason.
Your requests for support were met, even partly.
A post-mortem examined the conditions as well as your work.
Others in your role have hit the target and can describe how, and the criteria are in writing.
The missing information turned out to be unavailable to everybody.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Planners often underestimate how long things take, so the deadline may reflect a poor estimate.
Budgets get cut mid-quarter, and the person who assigned the task may have no say.
A busy person delegates with a thin brief because they do not have time to write a fuller one.
A manager can be unclear because the company is unclear, and vague goals often start with vague strategy.
common_false_positives: A start-up where everyone is stretched and the founder's own tasks are just as tight.
A coach's tough preparation set where the difficulty is the point and the athlete knows it.
A sales quota that is hard but hit by half the team.
discernment_questions: Could a competent person with these resources and this time have succeeded, and can I name someone who did?
Did I flag the constraints in writing before I began?
How were my requests for help handled, and how were other people's?
Can I write down what a pass looks like, and would the other person sign it?
Did the target move after I got near it?
When it failed, was the set-up discussed at all, or only me?
less_concerning_if: The shortfall in resources is shared by comparable tasks and acknowledged openly.
Requests for help get a real answer, even if the answer is no.
When you meet the target it is recognized, with no new condition appearing.
more_concerning_if: The same person hands you doomed tasks repeatedly while others get workable ones.
Your written flags of risk are ignored and the failure is then recorded as yours alone.
The record of misses is used to justify removing responsibility, pay, hours or a role.
pattern_over_time_signs: You begin sending a note in writing before each task listing what you would need.
Review meetings are mostly lists of what is missing.
You work longer hours each quarter for results that are no better received.
Colleagues or family members remember the failure but not its conditions.
Setting Up to Fail.repair_check: Repair starts with the retelling and the bar. A person who has noticed this goes back to the people who heard you failed, corrects the account to include the deadline and missing staff, and gives the next assignment the resources it needs or a pass line written down. Praise for effort that leaves the record unchanged is a different thing.
Setting Up to Fail.boundary_respect_check: Watch the next request you send. Ask in writing for what the task needs, or for the definition of done. A yes, a partial yes with a reason, or a clear no that is noted in the plan means you were taken seriously. A cheerful 'you'll manage' with no reply is another answer.
Setting Up to Fail.psychological_mechanism: Failure tends to be read as information about the person, and the conditions that produced it fade from memory faster than the outcome. If whoever set the task also describes the result, that account can become the accepted one. When a standard cannot be reached, effort stops translating into success, and people often turn the blame inward because the standard was presented as reasonable.
Setting Up to Fail.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe replaying the project to find what they should have done, working longer for less sense of achievement, and dreading review days and the next hand-off. Some start to believe they are bad at jobs they once did well, or stop volunteering ideas. Others say that writing down the original conditions brought a grim relief, because the failure looked different on paper.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask about the gap before starting: "This needs three people and I have one, with two weeks. What would you like me to put first?"
response_options.firm_boundary: Put your concerns on record: "I'll start, and I want it noted that without the client data this deadline is not realistic."
response_options.disengagement: Offer the version of the task that can be done and be plain about what is left out, rather than quietly absorbing the shortfall with unpaid overtime.
response_options.support_seeking: Walk a mentor or friend outside the project through the brief, deadline and resources, and ask whether they would have seen it as doable. Compare targets with peers in the same role.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Send a short written summary after the assignment conversation: scope, deadline, resources, what you asked for. Keep it for any review, and ask HR or a union representative how your targets compare with your peers'.

Setting Up to Fail.boundary_script: "I want this to go well, so I'm saying now that I can't finish it by Friday without the sales figures. Could we agree what counts as done, in writing, and when I can have the figures?"
Setting Up to Fail.safety_note: This is rarely a physical danger, but the record of misses can feed probation, dismissal, or job decisions that affect an immigration status or housing tied to the post. Keep the written brief, your flags and the outcome together, and ask a union representative, employment lawyer or legal aid service for advice before attending a disciplinary meeting alone.
misuse_warning: Calling every hard assignment a set-up can stop you learning from a failure that was partly yours. Ask whether the conditions were the same for others.
Treating a manager's vague wording as proof of a plan against you ignores that vagueness is often just an unfinished idea. Ask for specifics in writing first.
Setting Up to Fail.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Comparative Devaluation holds you up against other people; here the comparison is to a target nobody has met, or to unnamed peers who 'manage'. Shame Installation turns a failure into a judgment about who you are, whereas this tactic supplies the failures that judgment can feed on. Intimidation threatens consequences; here nothing is threatened, and the record carries the consequence.

Financial Control.short_definition: Restricting someone's access to money, financial information or earning, or using money and assets as leverage, so that they depend on one person.
Financial Control.core_meaning: Restricting someone's access to money, financial information or earning, or using money and assets as leverage, so that they depend on one person.
Financial Control.expanded_definition: Financial control is limiting what a person can see, spend, earn or own, or tying money and assets to behavior, so that disagreeing or leaving becomes costly. Financial enmeshment names this same lever, money and assets tied to compliance, so one entry covers both. Shared budgets and one-earner households are ordinary. The concern is money used as a lever: access given or withdrawn depending on compliance, information kept out of sight, and one name on everything.
Financial Control.plain_language_summary: One person decides what money you can see, spend or earn, and access shifts with how you behave, which makes it hard to disagree or to leave.
Financial Control.why_this_matters: Money decides whether a person can pay rent, buy food, hire a lawyer or leave a bad situation. When access depends on compliance, every disagreement carries a price, and the practical options narrow without anyone saying so out loud.
what_it_is: Limiting access to bank accounts, cards, statements or tax papers, so one person cannot see the household's real position.
Controlling earning: discouraging or forbidding work, or interfering with a job, a shift or a pay check.
Putting the home, the car, the accounts and the debts in one person's name only.
Handing out money as an allowance, a reward or a punishment, with asking required each time.
Finding loans, cards or debts in your name that you did not know about or agree to.
The opposite of transparent shared finances, where both people can see everything and neither can lock the other out.
what_it_sounds_like: "You don't need your own bank account."
"I'll decide what you get to spend."
"You're not allowed to work."
"My money, my rules."
"You'll get your allowance when you behave."
"Ask me for permission before you spend."
"Everything here is in my name."
"I'll cut off your card."
what_it_is_not: Agreed household budgeting where one person tracks the books and the other can see everything and change the arrangement.
A temporary arrangement during real hardship, discussed openly and with an end in sight.
A one-earner household with shared rules, where both people have access to the money.
Long-term financial interdependence built through a mutual relationship, which is common and not used as leverage.
A couple who agree to run big purchases past each other, in both directions.
A parent or guardian managing a minor's money, or an adult's money under a formal legal or care arrangement.
this_may_be_it_when: You cannot see statements or balances, or you are told you would not understand them.
Money for groceries, medicine or transport has to be requested, and may be refused after a disagreement.
Your earnings are taken over, or work is discouraged or interfered with.
Accounts, loans or signatures exist in your name that you never knowingly agreed to.
Money comes up in arguments as something you owe or could lose.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Both of you can see every account and change the arrangement whenever you like.
You chose the split for your own reasons and can spend your share without asking.
A restriction is time-limited and openly agreed, such as repaying a debt you both took on.
You have your own account or cash, and nothing is said when you use it.
When you ask to see papers, they are shown without fuss.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People differ in how they earn, spend and save, and a gap in style is not a gap in fairness.
One partner may simply be more comfortable with paperwork, and the other happy to leave it to them while seeing everything.
Family or cultural habits may have one person handle the money by long-standing, mutual agreement.
common_false_positives: A transparent shared budget in which both people can see everything and have a real say.
"My money, my rules" said as a joke inside a system where both people have access.
A couple living tightly while paying down a debt they chose together.
discernment_questions: Can I see every account, bill and loan I am named on, today, without asking permission?
If I wanted to spend a small amount on myself, would I need to explain or ask?
Could I cover rent and food for a month on my own if I needed to?
Does money come up in arguments as something that can be given or taken away?
Has anything been opened, borrowed or signed in my name that I did not agree to?
less_concerning_if: Both people can see all accounts, and the arrangement was chosen by both.
You have money of your own that nobody comments on.
Questions about money get answers and papers, not annoyance.
more_concerning_if: Money is withheld or granted depending on how you behave in an argument.
Work, school or contact with friends is discouraged in ways that leave you without income of your own.
Debts, loans or legal documents exist in your name without your informed agreement.
pattern_over_time_signs: Your own savings, income or credit shrink over time without a decision.
You ask for small amounts and keep track of what you have been given.
You rehearse how to raise a purchase, or put it off.
Documents you need, such as ID or bank cards, end up in someone else's keeping.
Financial Control.repair_check: Look for access that no longer depends on mood: your name on the accounts, statements you can open yourself, income that stays yours, and a way to see the whole picture. An apology after a hard conversation that leaves the same arrangement in place has changed the tone, not the control.
Financial Control.boundary_respect_check: Ask a small, practical question about money, such as to see last month's statement, and notice what comes next. Is the paper produced and the question treated as ordinary? Or does the answer turn to your tone, your motives, or what you owe?
Financial Control.psychological_mechanism: When a person cannot pay for food, travel or a lawyer without permission, going along can become the practical path of least resistance. Access that is granted and withdrawn can also teach a person to anticipate moods and avoid asking. Over time the narrowing of options can feel like a fact of life instead of an arrangement that someone could change.
Financial Control.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe asking permission for small purchases, hiding receipts, feeling like a child in their own home, and a sinking sense that leaving is not affordable. Some find out about debts only when a letter arrives. Others say the money was never the whole story, and that the loss of choices was what wore them down.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask an ordinary question in an ordinary tone: "Could we look at the statements together this weekend? I'd like to understand where we stand." If asking could make things worse, skip this step.
response_options.firm_boundary: If it feels safe, name the pattern once, calmly, without blame: "When money depends on how I behave, it is hard for me to speak up. Could we change that?" Otherwise take it to an advocate first.
response_options.disengagement: If a money conversation turns to what you owe or could lose, you can ask to pause it: "I need some time to think. Can we come back to this?" Use your own judgment about whether pausing is safe.
response_options.support_seeking: Speak to a domestic abuse advocate, a financial counselor or a legal aid service. Many can talk privately about economic abuse and help with documents, accounts and credit without the other person knowing.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If someone else controls your pay, ask payroll or HR in writing, when it is safe, whether wages can go to an account in your sole name. A legal aid or employment advice service can explain your rights.

Financial Control.boundary_script: "Could we go through the accounts together this weekend? I'd like both of us to be able to see what we have and agree who decides what." If asking could make things worse, skip it and call an advocate first.
Financial Control.safety_note: Warning signs include being cut off from money after you disagree, losing hold of your ID, phone or transport, debts opened in your name, or being kept from work. Quietly note what you know, and talk to a domestic abuse advocate or legal aid service about protecting income, documents and credit before you raise any change with the other person.
misuse_warning: Calling a tight budget, or one partner paying the bills, financial control can turn an agreed arrangement into an accusation. The test is whether the other person can see it and change it.
Using the label on a parent or guardian who manages a minor's or dependent adult's money under a formal arrangement mistakes protection for control.
Financial Control.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Infantilization treats you as unable to run your affairs in general, while financial control is specifically about who holds the money and the papers. "I Know Best" Paternalism overrides your choices for your own good and needs a stated reason; here the rule can be simply that the money is theirs. Isolation undermines your other relationships, whereas this limits the money needed to pay, travel or stay.
